p.src: The entertainment was held during a comparatively cold spell. The year was gradually drawing to its close. Spring lay less than twenty days ahead. Those who lived in the city were preparing to be busy. The burden of planning how to see in the New Year fell upon the poor. Amid all this, the entertainment welcomed everyone who was carefree, who had leisure to spare, and who knew no distinction between spring and year’s end. There were any number of them. Most were young men and women. On the first day, Yojirō cried out to Sanshirō that it was a tremendous success. Sanshirō had a ticket for the second day. Yojirō told him to invite Professor Hirota and take him along. When Sanshirō asked whether the professor’s ticket was not for a different day, Yojirō said that of course it was. But he explained that if the professor were left to himself, there was no chance at all that he would go, so Sanshirō must stop by and drag him out. Sanshirō agreed. When he went there in the evening, the professor had a large book spread open beneath a bright lamp. “Won’t you come?” Sanshirō asked. The professor smiled slightly and silently shook his head. It was a childlike gesture. Yet to Sanshirō it seemed scholarly. Perhaps it was the professor’s saying nothing that struck him as admirable. Sanshirō remained half-risen, at a loss. The professor felt sorry for having refused him. “If you’re going, I’ll come out with you. I’ll walk with you as far as the place.” The professor put on a black overcoat and went out. He seemed to have his hands tucked inside his coat, though Sanshirō could not be sure. The sky hung low. It was the sort of cold in which no stars could be seen. “It may rain.” “That would be troublesome, wouldn’t it?” “When people are going in and out, yes. Japanese theaters make people leave their footwear at the entrance, so they are terribly inconvenient even in fine weather.

p.src: “I prefer the open air. I want to see a beautiful play beneath a clear sky, neither hot nor cold, while breathing beautiful air. Surely one could create a pure and simple play, like the transparent air itself.” “If one of your dreams were made into a play, Professor, perhaps it would be like that.” “Do you know Greek drama?” “Not very well. They performed it outdoors, didn’t they?” “Outdoors. In broad daylight. It must have felt wonderful. The seats were natural stone. It was magnificent. Someone like Yojirō ought to be taken to such a place and shown a little of it.” Once again he was disparaging Yojirō. It was amusing to think that at this very moment Yojirō was inside the cramped hall, rushing about and making arrangements with all his might, immensely pleased with himself. If Sanshirō failed to bring the professor along, the professor would indeed not come. Yojirō would say that the professor had no idea how much good it would do him to visit a place like this once in a while, yet no matter how often he urged him, the professor would not listen. What a troublesome man. The certainty that he would sigh in just this fashion made it all the more amusing. The professor then gave him a detailed account of the structure of Greek theaters. At this point Sanshirō heard the professor expound such terms as “Theatron, Orchēstra, Skēnē, and Proskēnion.” He also learned that, according to some German scholar or other, the theater at Athens had seating for seventeen thousand people. That was one of the smaller ones. He heard that the largest could hold fifty thousand. He learned that there were two kinds of admission tokens, ivory and lead, both shaped rather like medals, with patterns stamped or designs engraved on their faces. The professor even knew the price of those admission tokens.

p.src: Electric lights blazed everywhere. People kept arriving in a steady stream. The turnout was even livelier than Yojirō had said. “Since you’ve come all this way, won’t you go in?” “No, I won’t.” The professor turned once more toward the darkness and walked away. Sanshirō watched the professor’s retreating figure for a while. Then he saw people arriving behind him by carriage and hurrying inside as though even the time it took to receive a footwear claim ticket were too precious to waste, and he too entered at a brisk pace. It was as though he had been pushed forward. Four or five men with nothing to do were standing at the entrance. One of them, a man in hakama, took his admission ticket. Peering into the hall over the man’s shoulder, he saw the space suddenly open out before him. It was also exceedingly bright. Sanshirō came close to shading his eyes with his hand as he took the seat to which he was shown. As he squeezed into the cramped space and looked around, his eyes dazzled at all the colors people had brought with them. It was not merely because he was moving his own eyes. It was because the colors clinging to countless people were forever moving through the vast space, each in its own separate, willful way. The performance onstage had already begun. Every character who appeared wore a court cap and formal shoes. Then a long palanquin was carried in. Someone stopped it in the middle of the stage. When the palanquin was lowered, another man emerged from within. The man drew his sword and began fighting the one who had pushed the palanquin back. —Sanshirō had no idea at all what was going on. To be sure, Yojirō had once told him the outline of the story. But he had listened only halfheartedly. Thinking he would understand once he saw it, he had merely said, “Ah, I see.” Yet now that he was watching it, he could not make the slightest sense of it. All that remained in Sanshirō’s memory was the name Minister Iruka. Sanshirō wondered which one was Iruka. There was no possible way to tell.

p.src: So he watched the entire stage as though it were Iruka. Before long, the caps, the shoes, the narrow-sleeved costumes, and even the language they used all began somehow to seem redolent of Iruka. In truth, Sanshirō had no definite conception of Iruka. It had been so long since he studied Japanese history that he had quite forgotten about Iruka of ancient times. It seemed as though it might have been in the time of Empress Suiko. Yet he felt it might just as well have been during the reign of Emperor Kinmei. He was certain, however, that it was neither Emperor Ōjin nor Emperor Shōmu. Sanshirō possessed only a vague feeling of Iruka-ness. Deciding that this was quite enough for watching a play, he gazed at the Tang-style costumes and scenery. But he could not follow the plot at all. Before long, the curtain fell.

p.src: Shortly before the curtain fell, the man beside him told the man on his other side that the actors spoke as though they were a parent and child conversing face-to-face in a six-mat room. He criticized them for having no training whatsoever. The man on that side said the actors lacked poise. He complained that every one of them was gangling and unsteady. Both men knew all the actors' real names by heart. Sanshirō listened closely to their conversation. They were both splendidly dressed. He supposed they were probably famous men. Yet he thought that if Yojirō heard this conversation, he would surely disagree. Just then someone behind them cried loudly, “Excellent, excellent—really excellent!” Both men beside him turned to look back. After that, they stopped talking altogether. Then the curtain fell. Here and there, people rose from their seats. From the hanamichi to the exits, figures hurried busily about. Sanshirō half rose and looked all around him. The person who was supposed to be there was nowhere in sight. In truth, he had kept as careful a watch as he could even during the performance. Since he had failed to spot her then, he had privately pinned his hopes on the interval. Sanshirō was a little disappointed. With no other choice, he turned his eyes back to the front. The men beside him apparently had a remarkably wide acquaintance; looking left and right, they would say who was sitting over there and who was sitting here, continually mentioning the names of well-known people. Among them were one or two with whom they exchanged greetings from a distance. Thanks to them, Sanshirō learned to recognize a few of these famous men's wives. One of them was newly married. She seemed a novelty even to one of his neighbors, for the man went to the trouble of wiping his spectacles again and gazed at her, saying, “I see, I see.” Then Yojirō came trotting from the far end toward them across the front of the curtained stage.

p.src: The man beside her had his back to Sanshirō. Sanshirō silently prayed that something might prompt the man to turn his way. Fortunately, the man stood up. Apparently weary of sitting, he perched on the partition of the box and began looking around the theater. At that moment Sanshirō could clearly make out Nonomiya's broad forehead and large eyes. When Nonomiya stood, Yoshiko, who had been behind Mineko, also came into view. Sanshirō tried to determine whether anyone else was with these three. But from that distance he could see only a dense mass of people; indeed, the entire pit looked like one great party, so there was no way to tell. Mineko and Yojirō seemed to exchange a few words from time to time. Nonomiya also appeared to join in now and then. Then Haraguchi suddenly emerged through the curtains. Standing beside Yojirō, he repeatedly peered into the pit. His mouth was surely moving as well. Nonomiya nodded as if in response to a signal. At that moment Haraguchi slapped Yojirō on the back with his open hand. Yojirō spun around, ducked beneath the bottom of the curtain, and vanished somewhere. Haraguchi climbed down from the stage, threaded his way between the spectators, and reached Nonomiya's side. Nonomiya raised himself to let Haraguchi pass. Haraguchi dropped neatly into the midst of the crowd. He disappeared from view near where Mineko and Yoshiko were sitting. Sanshirō, who had been watching every movement of this group with greater interest than he had shown in the performance, suddenly found himself envying Haraguchi's way of doing things. It had never occurred to him that one could approach someone by such a convenient method. He wondered whether he might try imitating it himself.

p.src: Before long, the curtain rose and Hamlet began. At Professor Hirota's house, Sanshirō had once seen a photograph of some famous Western actor playing Hamlet. The Hamlet who now appeared before Sanshirō was dressed in much the same fashion. And it was not only the costume. Even the face resembled it. Both wore the same knitted brows. This Hamlet moved with perfect agility, and it was delightful to watch. He moved vigorously about the stage and stirred it vigorously in turn. The effect was utterly different from Iruka performed in the style of Noh. Above all, whenever he stood center stage, spread his arms, or glared up at the heavens, he produced so powerful an effect that nothing else could find the slightest place in the spectators' field of vision. The lines, however, were in Japanese. It was Japanese translated from a Western language. The delivery rose and fell expressively. It had rhythm as well. Some passages flowed so smoothly that they seemed almost too eloquent. The language itself was magnificent. And yet it failed to carry him along. Sanshirō wished Hamlet would say something a little more Japanese. Just when he seemed about to say, “Mother, wouldn't that be a terrible wrong to Father?” he would suddenly bring in Apollo or someone of the sort and sail serenely on. Yet mother and son alike looked ready to burst into tears. Sanshirō, however, sensed this contradiction only dimly. He never found the courage to decide that the play was simply dull. Consequently, whenever he tired of Hamlet, he looked toward Mineko. Whenever Mineko disappeared behind someone and could no longer be seen, he watched Hamlet. p.src: The curtain fell again. Mineko and Yoshiko rose from their seats. Sanshirō rose after them. When he reached the corridor, he found the two women midway along it, talking to a man. The man had leaned half his body out through the doorway of the seats on the left, which could be entered directly from the corridor. The moment Sanshirō saw the man's profile, he turned back. Instead of returning to his seat, he collected his shoes and went outside. The night was dark by nature. Once he had passed beyond the places brightened by human hands, it seemed as though rain were falling. The wind rattled the branches. Sanshirō hurried back to his lodgings. It began raining at midnight. Lying in bed and listening to the rain, Sanshirō made the phrase “Get thee to a nunnery” into a pillar and wandered endlessly round and round it. Professor Hirota might still be awake too. What sort of pillar could the professor be embracing? Yojirō, on the other hand, must surely be lying insensible, buried in the vast darkness. …The next day, he had a slight fever. His head felt heavy, so he stayed in bed. At lunchtime he sat up in bed and ate. After sleeping once more, he awoke sweating. His mind grew hazy. Then Yojirō burst energetically into the room. He said Sanshirō had not been seen the previous evening and had apparently missed the morning lecture as well, so he had wondered what was wrong and come to check on him. Sanshirō thanked him. “Oh, I went last night. I did go. I even know perfectly well that you came out onto the stage and spoke to Mineko from a distance.” Sanshirō felt slightly intoxicated. Once he began speaking, the words slipped smoothly out. Yojirō reached out and pressed a hand to Sanshirō's forehead. “You've got quite a fever. You need to take some medicine. You've caught a cold.” “It was because the theater was much too hot and much too bright, and then, the moment I stepped outside, it was suddenly much too cold and much too dark.

When?” Yojirō still appeared unable to remember. Sanshirō had no choice but to explain in detail the circumstances surrounding the occasion. “Ah, yes, something like that may have happened,” Yojirō said. Sanshirō thought him terribly irresponsible. That sort of love belongs to the age of Yaoya Oshichi.” Sanshirō remained silent.

p.src: “The reason is this. Put a man and a woman of the same age, both around twenty, side by side. The woman has the upper hand in everything. The man can only be made a fool of. And a woman won’t feel inclined to marry a man she despises, will she? Women who think themselves the greatest people in the world are an exception, of course. If they refused to marry anyone they looked down on, they would have no choice but to remain single. You often see that sort among rich men’s daughters and the like: they willingly marry a man and then despise their husband. Mineko is far superior to that sort. But precisely for that reason, she would never consider marrying a man she could not respect as a husband, so anyone who sets his sights on her must bear that in mind. In that respect, neither you nor I am qualified to be her husband.” Sanshirō had ended up being lumped together with Yojirō. Yet he still said nothing. “Of course, you and I are both far superior to her. We may not look like much, but we are, you know. But it will take another five or six years before she can perceive the extent of our superiority. And there is no chance that she will sit quietly and wait for five or six years. Therefore, your marrying her is entirely ‘wind-horse-ox.’” Yojirō had used the compound “wind-horse-ox” in a peculiar place. Then he sat there laughing to himself. “Never mind. In another five or six years, someone far better than she is will come along. There is a surplus of women in Japan now, after all. There’s no point catching cold and running a fever over it. —The world is a wide place; there’s nothing to worry about. The truth is, I have various entanglements of my own, but she became such a nuisance that I told her I had to go to Nagasaki on business.” “What are you talking about?” “What do you think? A woman I’ve been involved with.” Sanshirō was astonished.

p.src: “So you must take your medicine and wait.” “Even after I’m well, I’ll stay in bed and wait.” The two laughed and parted. On his way out, Yojirō arranged for a nearby doctor to come. That evening, the doctor came. Since Sanshirō had no recollection of summoning a doctor himself, he was somewhat flustered at first. Presently the man took his pulse, and Sanshirō finally understood. He was a young and courteous man. Sanshirō judged him to be a substitute doctor. Five minutes later, the illness was diagnosed as influenza. He was instructed to take a dose of medicine that night and avoid exposure to the wind as much as possible. When he awoke the next day, his head felt considerably clearer. As long as he stayed in bed, he felt almost normal. But as soon as he lifted his head from the pillow, he grew dizzy. The maid came in and remarked that the room had grown quite stuffy with feverish heat. Without eating, Sanshirō lay on his back gazing at the ceiling. From time to time he drifted into a doze. He was plainly in the grip of fever and exhaustion. Remaining in their grip and offering no resistance, Sanshirō found a peculiar pleasure in yielding to nature as he drifted between sleep and wakefulness. He thought it was because his illness was mild. After four or five hours had passed, he gradually began to feel bored. He tossed and turned incessantly. The weather outside was fine. The sunlight on the shoji steadily shifted its shadows. Sparrows chirped. Sanshirō wished Yojirō would come and visit him again today. Just then the maid opened the shoji and announced that a lady had come to see him. He had not expected Yoshiko to come so soon. It was just the sort of swift work one could expect from Yojirō. Still lying down, he fixed his eyes on the open doorway; before long, a tall figure appeared on the threshold. Today she was wearing purple hakama. Both her feet remained in the corridor. She seemed to hesitate for a moment before entering. Sanshirō raised his shoulders from the bed and said, “Welcome.”

p.src: Yoshiko closed the shoji and sat down beside his pillow. The six-mat room was already in disarray, and since it had not been cleaned that morning, it felt more cramped than ever. “Stay in bed,” she said to Sanshirō. Sanshirō laid his head back on the pillow. He alone was perfectly at ease. “Doesn't it smell?” he asked. “Yes, a little,” she replied, though she showed no particular sign of finding it unpleasant. “Do you have a fever? What can your illness be? Has the doctor been?” “The doctor came last night. He says it's influenza.” “Sasaki came early this morning and said, ‘Ogawa is ill, so please go and visit him. I don't know what the illness is, but it seems to be anything but mild.’ That startled both Mineko and me.” Yojirō had exaggerated a little again. Put unkindly, it was as though he had used this ruse to lure Yoshiko out. Sanshirō was so good-natured that he felt terribly sorry for her. “Thank you very much,” he said as he lay there. Yoshiko took a basket of mandarins from her cloth-wrapped bundle. “Mineko reminded me, so I bought them,” she admitted candidly. It was hard to tell which of them the visit was really from. Sanshirō offered Yoshiko his thanks all the same. “Mineko was supposed to come too, but she has been rather busy lately—she asked me to give you her regards...” “Has something special arisen to keep her busy?” “Yes. Something has,” she said. Her large black eyes rested on Sanshirō's face upon the pillow. From below, Sanshirō looked up at Yoshiko's pale forehead. He remembered long ago, when he had first met her at the hospital. Even now she looked languid. At the same time, she was cheerful. She had brought to Sanshirō's bedside every comfort upon which he could rely.

p.src: “It's delicious, isn't it? It's Mineko's gift for your recovery.” “I've had enough.” She took a white handkerchief from her sleeve and wiped her hands. “Mr. Nonomiya, what became of your marriage proposal?” “Nothing more came of it.” “I hear Mineko has received a proposal too, hasn't she?” “Yes, it has already been settled.” “Who is the man?” “The gentleman who said he wanted to marry me. Ho, ho, ho—isn't it funny? He's a friend of Mineko's elder brother. Before long, my brother and I will set up house together again. Once Mineko leaves, I can't very well go on imposing on them.” “Aren't you going to marry?” “I will, if only I find somewhere I want to go.” With that, she laughed lightheartedly. Clearly, there was nowhere she wanted to go yet. From that day on, Sanshirō remained in bed for about four days. On the fifth day, he ventured apprehensively into the bath and looked in the mirror. He had the face of a dead man. He steeled himself and went to the barber. The following day was Sunday. After breakfast, he put on several shirts and an overcoat to keep out the cold, then went to Mineko's house. Yoshiko was standing in the entrance hall, just about to step down onto the place where shoes were removed. She said she was just setting out for her brother's place. Mineko was not at home. Sanshirō went outside with Yoshiko. “Are you completely well now?” “Thank you. I'm all better now. —Where has Satomi gone?” “My brother?” “No, I mean Mineko.” “Mineko has gone to church.” It was the first Sanshirō had heard of Mineko going to church. After learning which church it was, Sanshirō parted from Yoshiko. After turning through some three side streets, he found himself directly in front of it. Sanshirō was a man with absolutely no connection to Christianity. He had never even peered inside a church. He stood in front of it and looked up at the building.

Then I'll keep it.” She slipped the paper parcel inside her robe. When she withdrew her hand from her azuma coat, she was holding a white handkerchief. She held it to her nose and looked at Sanshirō. She seemed to be smelling the handkerchief. Then she suddenly extended that hand. The handkerchief came before Sanshirō's face. A sharp fragrance struck him. “Heliotrope,” she said quietly. Sanshirō instinctively drew back his face. The bottle of heliotrope perfume. Twilight in the Fourth District. Stray sheep. Stray sheep. High in the sky, the sun shone brightly. “I hear you're getting married.” Mineko let the white handkerchief fall into her sleeve. “You know about it?” she said, narrowing her double-lidded eyes as she looked at his face. It was a look that held Sanshirō at a distance, yet showed an almost excessive concern for how far away he was. And yet her brows alone remained distinctly composed. Sanshirō's tongue stuck to the roof of his mouth. After gazing at Sanshirō for some time, she faintly let out a sigh so soft it was barely audible. Then she raised her slender hand to her dark brows and said: “For I acknowledge my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me.” Her voice was almost too faint to hear. Yet Sanshirō heard every word clearly. And so Sanshirō and Mineko parted. When he returned to his lodgings, a telegram from his mother was waiting for him. He opened it and read: “When are you leaving?”

She seemed to be smelling the handkerchief.
Then she suddenly extended that hand.
The handkerchief came before Sanshirō's face.
A sharp fragrance struck him.
“Heliotrope,” she said quietly.
Sanshirō instinctively drew back his face.
The bottle of heliotrope perfume.
Twilight in the Fourth District.
Stray sheep.
Stray sheep.
High in the sky, the sun shone brightly.
“I hear you're getting married.” Mineko let the white handkerchief fall into her sleeve.
“You know about it?” she said, narrowing her double-lidded eyes as she looked at his face.
It was a look that held Sanshirō at a distance, yet showed an almost excessive concern for how far away he was.
And yet her brows alone remained distinctly composed.
Sanshirō's tongue stuck to the roof of his mouth.
After gazing at Sanshirō for some time, she faintly let out a sigh so soft it was barely audible.
Then she raised her slender hand to her dark brows and said:
“For I acknowledge my transgressions,
and my sin is ever before me.” Her voice was almost too faint to hear.
Yet Sanshirō heard every word clearly.
And so Sanshirō and Mineko parted.
When he returned to his lodgings, a telegram from his mother was waiting for him.
He opened it and read: “When are you leaving?”
